det.description: MegaDetector is an object detection model that identifies animals, people, and vehicles in camera trap images (which also makes it useful for eliminating blank images). This model is trained on several hundred thousand bounding boxes from a variety of ecosystems. The animals located by this model with be further identified by the species recognition models.

MegaDetector 5b differs from 5a only in its training data and is also an object detection model that identifies animals, people, and vehicles in camera trap images (which also makes it useful for eliminating blank images). This model is trained on several hundred thousand bounding boxes from a variety of ecosystems. The animals located by this model with be further identified by the species recognition models.

This model is a new addition to the MegaDetector series, designed to improve accuracy, but still needs to be thoroughly tested by the community. These are object detection models designed to identify animals, people, and vehicles in camera trap images. Animals detected by this model will be passed to species recognition models for further identification. By default, if you're already using MDv5a or MDv5b, keep using it until you have time to do a thorough comparison on your data against MDv1000-redwood. If you're starting from scratch and you want the safe thing that has been studied extensively in the literature, use MDv5a. If you want to join me on the cutting edge and see some bananas-good recall, use MDv1000-redwood. Only use the smaller model MDv1000-spruce if you're sure you need them. Faster sounds better, but in a world where a regular laptop with no GPU can process 50k images per day even through MDv5, and GPUs than can do 1M images per day come standard on home PCs now, the scenario where speed makes a qualitative difference is niche, and if in practice running 2x faster means you need to lower your confidence threshold to preserve recall, you've reduced compute time to increase human time, which is almost never a tradeoff you want to make.
det.description_short: Promising new standard • Not battle tested yet

cls.description: SpeciesNet is an image classifier designed to accelerate the review of images from motion-triggered wildlife cameras ('camera traps'). This classifier was trained at Google using a large dataset of camera trap images and an EfficientNet V2 M architecture (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00574). It is designed to classify images into one of more than 2000 labels, covering diverse animal species, higher-level taxa (like 'mammalia' or 'felidae'), and non-animal classes ('blank', 'vehicle'). AddaxAI automatically combines SpeciesNet with MegaDetector (https://github.com/agentmorris/MegaDetector) using a set of heuristics, geofencing rules and taxonomic aggregation that take into account the geographical origin of the image to improve the reliability of its species classification.

The Deepfaune initiative aims at developing 'artificial intelligence' models to automatically classify species in images and videos collected using camera-traps. The initiative is led by a core academic team from the French 'Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique' (CNRS), in collaboration with more than 50 European partners involved in wildlife research, conservation and management. The Deepfaune models can be run through a custom software freely available on the website, or through other software packages or platforms like EcoAssist. New versions of the model are published regularly, increasing classification accuracy or adding new species to the list of species that can be recognized. More information is available at: https://www.deepfaune.cnrs.fr

The Sub-Saharan Drylands model is a deep learning image classifier trained on > 2.8 million camera trap images from diverse ecosystems across eastern and southern Africa. Covering 328 categories, primarily at the species level, it supports taxonomic fallback, predicting higher-level taxa (e.g., genus or family) when species-level certainty is low. The model is designed for wildlife identification across savannas, dry forests, arid shrublands, and semi-desert habitats. Training data includes images from South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya, Mozambique, Botswana, Namibia, Rwanda, Madagascar, and Uganda. All training images are open-source and available via LILA BC (https://lila.science/).
cls.description_short: East & Southern Africa savannas • 328 classes • Trained on 2.8M images

cls.description: This model intends to support Bengal tiger conservation by classifying 10 categories of animals present in the Terai region of Nepal. The model was trained on about 2,000 images per class (source: LILA BC, https://lila.science/). The overall F1 score is 0.935 on a held-out test set (250 images per class), though performance varies somewhat by class. Local images from Nepal were not available so that images of visually similar 'substitute' species had to be used, i.e. the model's ability to generalize to the target region remains to be tested. The model is based on a pre-trained EfficientNetV2M. Image preparation (relying on MegaDetector) and model training follow MEWC.

The MEWC model for Tasmania has been trained on 2.5 million labelled images from 96 classes. It is based on the EfficientNet v2 Small model architecture, initialised with pre-trained ImageNet base weights. The classes include all non-volant terrestrial mammals (native and introduced) that are found in Tasmania, along with over 50 of the most-commonly observed bird species seen on camera traps. Most classes represent species, but there are also some general classes like snake or insect, and an unknown/washed-out special class. Based on held-out test data, the overall classification accuracy and f1 scores are >99%, and for the common species, accuracy typically exceeds 99.5%. The results for the rarest taxa are worse, but still over 90% in almost all cases.
Model to identify 30 species or higher level taxons present in the desert biome of the Skeleton Coast National Park, North Namibia. The model was trained on a set of more than 850,000 images.

Model to identify 17 species or higher-level taxons present in New Zealand. The model was trained on a set of approximately 2 million camera trap images from various projects across the country. These projects were run by multiple organizations and took place in a diverse range of habitats, using a variety of trail camera brands and models. The model has an overall validation accuracy, precision, and recall of 98%. When tested on an out-of-sample test set, the model scored 95%, 96%, and 94%, respectively. The model was designed to expedite the monitoring of New Zealand's invasive species (deer, possum, pig, cat, rodent, and mustelid).
This model was trained by Mathias Tobler from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Information about the source of the training dataset and model metrics is not available.
cls.description_short: 53 classes • San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance

cls.description: Model to identify 14 species or higher-level taxons present in Southern Turkmenistan. The model was trained on a set of approximately 1 million camera trap images. The model has an overall validation accuracy, precision, and recall of 95%, 93%, and 94%, respectively. The accuracy was not tested on an out-of-sample-dataset since local images were absent.
cls.description_short: Southern region • 14 classes • Trained on 1M images

cls.description: This model is dedicated to the classification of the fauna from Kirghizistan. It was developped by Hex Data (https://hex-data.io) on behalf of OSI-Panthera (https://www.osi-panthera.org/). The model was trained on 42k images, with around 4k images per class, provided by the camera traps set up by OSI-Panthera. Class 'vide' (empty, in French), is used to try to set aside the few false negatives returned by MegaDetector. The rest correspond to the scientific name of the family or species detected.
cls.description_short: Manas v1 • OSI-Panthera • Trained on 42k images

cls.description: This model distinguishes between 27 species native to the Southwest United States. The training data was collected partially by SDZWA and the California Mountain Lion Project, and includes examples from the NACTI, and CCT training datasets. The training data corpus comprises 91662 images. We used a 70/20/10 Train/Val/Test split. The model reached an overall accuracy of 88% on the test set. Created by Kyra Swanson in 2023 (tswanson@sdzwa.org).

This model distinguishes between 51 species and groups found across the western United States, and expands the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance's Southwest USA model to the whole region. It was trained on 555,668 images, mostly from LILA datasets (https://lila.science), and reached an overall accuracy of 94.9% on a 46,238 image evaluation set. Created by Kyra Swanson and Raine Wen (San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance) in 2026.

This model classifies 13 species or higher taxonomic groups found in the Kuraiyama Experimental Forest (KEF) of Gifu University. It was trained on approximately 23,000 camera trap images collected through a wildlife monitoring project in KEF. The model was developed to support the efficient monitoring of key wildlife species in central Japan, sika deer, wild boar, Asian black bear, and Japanese serow. The class-wise accuracies for these four representative species are as follows: deer 0.97, boar 0.94, black bear 0.82, and serow 0.88. Please note that the model was trained on data limited to KEF and its surrounding area, and it has not yet undergone a comprehensive accuracy evaluation. The training data is also limited and imbalanced. This model is intended as a prototype for future development of models for classifying wild animals in Japan.The image dataset used to train this model is the same as the one used in Ando et al. (2019). However, data of humans and dogs were not used for training. Ando et al. (2019) Recognition of wildlife using deep learning in images taken by camera traps. Mammalian Science. 59(1):49-60.(In Japanese with English summary)
cls.description_short: 13 classes • prototype on limited, imbalanced data • very biased to deer

cls.description:
The AI Puaʻa Initiative develops artificial intelligence models to automatically classify wildlife species in camera trap imagery collected across Hawaiʻi, with a focus on introduced and managed species. The initiative is led through a collaboration between The Nature Conservancy (TNC), the USDA Forest Service Pacific Southwest Research Station, Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry (IPIF), the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Wildlife Ecology and Management Lab, the Hawaiʻi Division of Forestry and Wildlife (DOFAW), and Addax Data Science, with contributions from conservation practitioners and community-based monitoring efforts. The AI Puaʻa models are trained on datasets collectively pooled and curated from camera trap deployments across the State of Hawaiʻi, representing the variation in species encountered in local monitoring efforts. These models improve classification accuracy for species that are often underrepresented or inconsistently identified in generalized wildlife models trained outside of Hawaiʻi. Models developed through this initiative are accessible through the Addax AI platform, providing a cost-effective and user-friendly solution for processing and analyzing camera trap data without requiring advanced technical expertise or reliance on expensive proprietary or subscription-based software.

New versions of the model will be released as additional data become available, improving classification performance and expanding species coverage over time.
cls.description_short: AI Puaʻa v1.0 • 15 classes • USDA Forest Service & TNC
cls.owner: USDA Forest Service – Pacific Southwest Research Station, Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry (IPIF) & The Nature Conservancy (TNC)

cls.description: This model distinguishes between 212 species (both indigenous and introduced) found within the state of Victoria, Australia and was designed to expedite camera trap monitoring. The model was trained on a set of approximately 5 million camera trap images from various projects across Victoria. The training dataset was curated by Parks Victoria, with images submitted by more than 30 different research and conservation organisations. Efforts were made to ensure the training library was representative of species' home ranges across Victoria's 28 bioregions. Images were taken with a variety of trail camera brands and models and camera set-ups. Where insufficient Victorian images existed for a species (e.g. Spot-tailed Quoll), images were sourced from neighbouring Australian states. The model was trained using a fine-tuned SpeciesNet architecture on 5.0M samples, 49.4K locations, and 212 classes.
cls.developer: Addax Data Science for Parks Victoria

cls.description:
This model distinguishes between 68 species native to the Southwestern United States and the U.S-Mexico Borderlands region. It was trained using a fine-tuned SpeciesNet architecture. Training data totaling 775K images were collected in Arizona, California, and Texas by nearly 20 collaborators (see Acknowledgements) and combined with 2.3M publicly available images from a total of 8K camera locations. We used a 70/20/10 train/validation/test split based on location. The model reached an overall accuracy of 94% on the test set. 

Acknowledgements: 
This model was developed with support of a U.S Fish and Wildlife Service, Tribal Wildlife Grant (no. F22AP01262-00) to the Tohono O'odham Nation, Department of Natural Resources, Wildlife and Vegetation Management Program and collaborator Dr. Aaron D. Flesch of the University of Arizona, School of Natural Resources and the Environment. Kinley Ragan of the Arizona Center for Nature Conservation/Phoenix Zoo provided extensive help with data management and quality control in support of model development, and Peter van Lunteren of Addax Data Science developed the model. cls.description: This model was developed to classify wildlife captured by close-focus, downward-facing camera traps used in the Adapted Hunt Drift Fence Technique (AHDriFT; Martin et al. 2017; Amber et al. 2021). The model is based on a fine-tuned SpeciesNet architecture and was trained on data collected in Ohio, USA: 118,554 images from 1,169 camera trap locations, 46 classes; available at the LILA BC repository, https://lila.science/datasets/ohio-small-animals/. We used a 72/18/10 Train/Val/Test split by camera trap location to ensure spatial independence between splits. The model achieved an overall accuracy of 83.6% on the held-out test set. Taxonomic fallback is supported, allowing predictions to be assigned to higher taxonomic levels when species-level confidence is below a user-defined threshold. Regular updates of AHDriFT-ID are planned. Users are encouraged to contribute labeled AHDriFT image datasets via https://lila.science/ to support future model updates. Contact: Greg Lipps (lipps.37@osu.edu)
cls.developer: The Ohio State University, Columbus Zoo and Aquarium, Addax Data Science

cls.description: This species recognition model was developed to automate and enhance camera trap monitoring effort across the forested landscapes of Central India. Built on a fine-tuned SpeciesNet architecture, the model is designed to classify 40 distinct classes using a robust dataset of 1.1 million samples collected from 10,300 unique locations. The training data spans a diverse range of habitats, primarily focusing on the dry and moist deciduous forests characteristic of the region. Approximately 70% of this dataset consists of proprietary data curated by the Wildlife Conservation Trust (WCT), featuring images captured using systematically deployed, ground-based, horizontally oriented camera traps positioned at optimized heights to maximize the detection zone for a wide array of species. The remaining 30% consists of supplemental data sourced from LILA BC, a public archive of camera trap imagery which was utilized to bolster underrepresented classes where local data was limited, thereby ensuring high classification accuracy across all categories.
cls.description_short: Fine-tuned SpeciesNet • 40 classes • Trained on 1.1M images

cls.description:
This species recognition model was developed for camera trap monitoring in the tropical savannas of the Northern Territory, Australia. It includes both native and introduced vertebrate species and was trained on approximately 890,000 images, about 70% of which were curated by Charles Darwin University, Territory Natural Resource Management, and Warddeken Land Management. Training data span a range of habitats, including lowland savanna forest and woodland, sandstone escarpment, roads, and coastal areas. Images were collected from ground-based, horizontally oriented Reconyx camera traps. The remaining 30% were sourced from LILA BC, a public archive of camera trap imagery, to supplement classes where local data were limited.

The model is fine-tuned from the SpeciesNet backbone and outputs 140-class predictions. It is optimized with a taxonomic aggregation strategy to return classifications at multiple levels of the taxonomic hierarchy (species, genus, family, order and class) to enhance accuracy, flexibility and generalizability.

The underlying raw image data are not publicly available due to access restrictions. The curating organisations recognise the Indigenous Data Sovereignty rights of Traditional Owners across the Top End, on whose Country these species persist, and pay their respects to Elders past and present, and acknowledge their ongoing role in supporting conservation and land management in the region.
cls.description_short: Fine-tuned SpeciesNet • 140 classes • Trained on 890k images
cls.owner: Charles Darwin University, Territory Natural Resource Management, Warddeken Land Management

cls.description: This model distinguishes between 53 species native to the Peruvian Andes. The training data was collected by SDZWA and comprises 201,943 images. We used a 70/20/10 Train/Val/Test split. The model reached an overall accuracy, precision, and recall of 88.9%, 88.6%, and 87.3% respectively on the test set.

The wildobs_QLD_WetTropics model for Australian Wet Tropics has been trained on ~30k labelled images from 15 classes. We used the Wildlife Observatory of Australia’s tagged image repository for the ‘Wet Tropics’ rainforests (n = 454 camera deployments, 2,184,664 images, 121 species), and refined this to a balanced dataset of the 15 most common species for CV training and testing. We found that fine-tuning SpeciesNet (https://github.com/google/cameratrapai) delivered the highest performance, often exceeding 95% F1-score. We are in the process of publishing our findings as part of this work.
cls.developer: Prakash Palanivelu Rajmohan and Renuka Sharma

cls.description: Model AWC135 was designed to increase the efficiency of processing images from motion cameras, by creating an Australian specific model that contains a diverse range of common, threatened, and invasive species. This model classifies 135 labels of Australian species from 33 different source locations across the country. Several grouped labels were created with images from two or more species for either visually similar animals (e.g. 'Grey Kangaroo sp' contains images of both Eastern and Western Grey Kangaroos), or low importance/low abundance species (e.g. 'Wetland Bird sp' contains images of 15 different waterbird species such as Herons, Ibis, and Bush-hens). As a result of these grouped labels, images from over 200 species are included across the 135 labels. Majority of images used were sourced from AWC's internal repository. Additional images were shared by several partnership collaborators. A candidate set of 1.5 million images were verified for correct ID and appropriate quality by an ecologist, resulting in a training set of ~1.1 million images. Model AWC135 achieves a macro average F1 score of 95% on the top 108 species, and 91% across all 135 species, on the held-out test set. This project is funded by the Australian Government Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The project is led by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy and undertaken in partnership with: Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation; Kakadu National Park / Parks Australia; NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service; Ngalurrtju Aboriginal Land Trust and the Central Land Council; South Australian Government Department of Primary Industries and Regions; the University of Melbourne; Wilinggin Aboriginal Corporation.

Model to identify 81 species or higher-level taxons present in New Zealand. The model was trained on a set of camera trap images from various projects across the country. These projects were run by multiple organizations and took place in a diverse range of habitats, using a variety of trail camera brands and models. When tested on a balanced out-of-sample test set of 6,372 images, the model scored 0.90 and 0.95 for balanced accuracy and macro average precision, respectively. The model was designed to expedite the monitoring of New Zealand species, including native species.

TropiCam-AI is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained to classify arboreal mammal and bird species in the Neotropical region from camera-traps deployed in the tree canopy. It was trained using a ConvNeXt-Base architecture on ~189.000 camera-trap images from several deployments in Neotropical countries (Brazil, Peru, French Guiana, Costa Rica) and augmented with ~54.000 citizen-science images gathered from the iNaturalist platform. It is designed to work in conjunction with the MegaDetector algorithm, in the well-established two-stage detection and classification pipeline. TropiCam-AI can recognize a total of 84 taxa, and it was optimized with a taxonomic aggregation strategy to return classification at multiple levels of the taxonomy hierarchy (e.g. species, genus, family, class and order) to enhance accuracy, flexibility and generalizability to unseen locations and species. TropiCam-AI was released with the publication “Introducing TropiCam-AI: A taxonomically flexible automated classifier of Neotropical arboreal mammals and birds from camera-trap data” (https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70213). Further information can be found on the dedicated GitHub repository (https://github.com/andrewzamp/TropiCam-AI).
cls.developer: Andrea Zampetti, National Museum of Natural Sciences (MNCN-CSIC), Madrid, Spain

cls.description: One objective of the OneForestVision initiative is to develop open-source artificial intelligence models for biodiversity monitoring. DeepForestVision automatically classifies species in images and videos collected using camera-traps in African tropical forests. It is developed by an academic team from the French Muséum National d'Histore Naturelle (MNHN), in collaboration with 6 partners involved in wildlife research, conservation and management. DeepForestVision can be run through AddaxAI without programming knowledge, or downloaded on the project Github page https://github.com/MNHN-OFVI/DeepForestVision.
cls.developer: Hugo Magaldi - One Forest Vision initiative

cls.description: DeepForestVision v2, the successor to v1, from the One Forest Vision initiative. It automatically classifies species in camera-trap images and videos from African tropical forests, using a DINOv3 (ViT-B/16) backbone. Developed by the French Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle (MNHN) with partners in wildlife research, conservation and management. It can be run through AddaxAI without programming knowledge, or downloaded from the project GitHub page https://github.com/MNHN-OFVI/DeepForestVisionV2.
cls.developer: Hugo Magaldi - One Forest Vision initiative

cls.description: This model was previously named 'Columbian Amazon'. The model is trained to classify animals into their genus taxonomic group. The training data are collected by the Department of Biological sciences at Universidad de los Andes. All the images come from the 'Magdalena Medio' region in Colombia. The dataset contains 41,904 images across 36 labeled genera, and it is distributed into 33,569 images in the training set and 8,335 images in the validation set. In our inference of the Amazon Rainforest dataset, we implement a 98% confidence threshold as part of a human-in-the-loop procedure. We observe that the model predicts 90% of the data with recognition confidence exceeding this threshold. Furthermore, within this high-confidence subset, the model achieves an average classification accuracy of 92%. This means that, after filtering out empty images with MegaDetector, only 10% of the detected animal objects require human validation.

This model classifies animals in images from small-animal camera traps: downward-facing, close-focus cameras that look into a baited box or tray. It was trained on the California Small Animals dataset from California Department of Fish and Wildlife, available at the LILA BC repository, https://lila.science/datasets/california-small-animals/. That dataset holds 2,278,071 images from 701 camera locations, and its 257 source categories were merged into 29 classes: 27 animal groups plus blank and setup_pickup. The classes are groups rather than species, for example mouse, vole, whiptail or spiny_lizard, because the source labels were merged where the animals cannot be told apart in these images. Train and validation were split by camera location, so no camera appears on both sides. The backbone is a fine-tuned EVA-02 large vision transformer at 448 pixels. This is a full-image classifier: it reads the whole frame, so MegaDetector does not run and the results carry no bounding boxes and no counts per image. Expect roughly one image per second on a laptop CPU, and much faster on a GPU.

emb.description: DINOv2 small vision transformer (ViT-S/14) trained with self-supervised learning by Meta AI. Produces 384-dimensional feature vectors for detection crops. This is the fastest variant (21M parameters) and the recommended starting point for most camera trap projects. It processes crops roughly 2.5x faster than ViT-B and 7x faster than ViT-L, while still capturing enough visual detail for similarity search and clustering. Ideal for large datasets with hundreds of thousands of detections.

DINOv2 base vision transformer (ViT-B/14) trained with self-supervised learning by Meta AI. Produces 768-dimensional feature vectors for detection crops. This is the mid-range variant (86M parameters), roughly 2.5x slower than ViT-S but with higher-dimensional embeddings that capture finer visual distinctions. Consider this model if you need better discrimination and have a GPU available.

DINOv2 large vision transformer (ViT-L/14) trained with self-supervised learning by Meta AI. Produces 1024-dimensional feature vectors for detection crops. This is the largest variant (300M parameters), roughly 7x slower than ViT-S. It offers the highest embedding quality but with diminishing returns over ViT-B. Best suited for small datasets or research workflows where maximum discriminative power justifies the extra compute time. A GPU is strongly recommended.
